body.p: I. Introduction

The undersigned thanks Examiner Yankey for review and consideration of the present Application. In response to the Office Action of June 5, 2024 ("Office Action"), the undersigned submits the present amendment and remarks ("Response").

Upon entry of the present amendment, claims 24-31 and 33-40 will be pending in this application. Claims 24, 29, 37, and 38 have been amended, and claims 1-23, 32, and 41 have been canceled. No new matter is added. Based on the following remarks, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and allowance of the pending claims. II. Claim Rejections under 35 U.S.C. " 102 & 103

Claims 38-40 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as allegedly being anticipated by U.S. Patent Publication No. 2015/0360783 Al to Cailleteau et al. ("Cailleteau"). Claims 24 and 29-31 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as allegedly being anticipated by or, in the alternative under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Publication No. 2013/0248655 Al to Kroll et al. ("Kroll"). Claims 25-27 and 32 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Kroll as applied to claim 24 above, in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2018/0281963 to Dowty et al. ("Dowty"). Claims 24-36 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Dowty in view of Kroll, in view of Cailleteau. Claim 37 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Dowty in view of Kroll, in view of Cailleteau as applied to claim 24 above, in view of U.S. Patent No. 5,024,398 to Riedinger et al. ("Riedinger"). Claims 38-40 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as allegedly being anticipated by Dowty or, in the alternative, 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Dowty in view of Cailleteau. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration as explained below.
A. Claim 24

Applicant respectfully submits that the prior art fails to teach or suggest at least "the front side of the storage unit provides access from the interior of the aircraft passenger seat unit to the holders of the storage unit" and "the door is arranged to slide between the first position and the second position" as recited in claim 24.

Referring to the below figure, in one instance, the Office Action rejects claim 24 in view of Kroll, alleging that Kroll discloses a seat 28, a privacy shell 24, 36, 38 with an opening, a storage unit 60 (shown in below figure but not numbered), and a door 66 (shown in below figure but not numbered). Office Action pages 5-6.

Kroll teaches a door 66 that is pivotally attached to a tray 62 that is part of a storage compartment 60 that is integrated into a privacy wall. Therefore, the door 66 is not a door that slides between the first and second position, as is now required by claim 24.

Moreover, the skilled person would find no motivation whatsoever to modify the door of Kroll such that it is a sliding door. Firstly, Kroll teaches against the implementation of a sliding door, as Kroll teaches in paragraph [0055] that it is preferable for the door to swing "open in the direction away from the passenger so that the mirror faces the passenger." Such an arrangement would not be possible with a sliding door, and thus the skilled person would be taught against implementing a sliding door. Even if, for sake of argument (and which Applicant does not concede) the skilled person were to modify the door of Kroll to be a sliding door, they would have no motivation to modify to door of Kroll to somehow be a sliding door such that is "movable in relation to the storage unit between a first position in which the door at least partially blocks off the primary opening, and a second position in which the door at least partially closes access to holders of the storage unit" (emphasis added) as recited in claim 24.

Incorporating such a sliding door into the storage compartment 60 appears to be impossible, as the storage compartment 60 is designed to be mounted "substantially flush with the privacy wall" and is "shaped to follow the curvature of the privacy wall" (see paragraph [0054] of Kroll), and there is no teaching or suggestion to somehow provide a door with the first and second positions as claimed. Therefore, at least for these reasons claim 24 as amended is novel and inventive in view of Kroll.
In another instance, the Office Action rejects claim 24 based on the combination of Dowty, Kroll, and Cailleteau. Office Action page 10.

Claim 24 unambiguously requires that access is provided from the front side of the storage unit into the interior of the passenger seat unit. Claim 24 now differs from Dowty in particular, in that the access point is on the inside of the passenger accommodation unit rather than the aisle side of the privacy shell per the teachings of Dowty. This has the effect that the door used to at least partially block access to the aircraft seat unit in a first position may also, in that first position, provide access to a storage unit such that said storage unit may be accessed by a passenger from within the passenger seat unit. Thus, the seat unit provides private storage for the passenger (see page 1 lines 20 and 21 of the application).

As set forth in the previous response, Dowty does not disclose a passenger seat unit with an individual storage unit. Instead, the seat units of Dowty can include forward cabin monuments which can be various types of cabin furniture, such as a storage compartment, and may have an aisle-side opening. The forward cabin monument can include "galley compartments" and "electronics compartments" (paragraph [0003]), which would be accessible by aircraft staff, and therefore be accessed from the aisle (rather than from inside a passenger seat unit as claimed). There is no suggestion in Dowty that an entrance to a forward cabin monument could be moved, or that it would be desirable to do so.

Moreover, claim 24 requires that the front side of the storage unit provides access from the interior the aircraft passenger seat unit to the holders of the storage unit. Therefore, the door of Dowty, in the most relevant embodiment of Dowty, to which the skilled person would turn, cannot be used to block access to the storage compartment, as required by the claim.

Further, claim 24 requires that the font side of the storage unit provides access from the interior of the aircraft passenger seat unit to the holders of the storage unit. In contrast, and with reference to the annotated figure provided by the Office Action (reproduced below), the alleged

"front side" of Dowty's storage unit provides access from the exterior of the aircraft passenger seat unit, and therefore the Office Action's construction of Fig. 26E of Dowty to somehow read on claim 24 is no longer possible.

In addition, as the cabin monument of Dowty is a pre-existing feature of the aircraft interior that passenger suites must be designed around, the skilled person would not find modifying the cabin monument practicable, let alone desirable. Such fixtures in an aircraft may have structural features that cannot be safely or easily altered. Such alterations would also have to be reversed if the seating arrangement of the aircraft were changed at a later date. The skilled person is a designer of aircraft passenger accommodation units and would understand that these passenger accommodation units are designed to fit around preexisting structural features of the aircraft cabin. Paragraphs [0003] and [0008] of Dowty explain that the design of front row passenger suites is adapted around the forward cabin monument. Thus, there is no reason for the skilled person to consider adapting the forward cabin monument itself, as the teaching of Dowty is to design the passenger suite around the cabin monument.

Additionally, claim 1 requires that the storage unit is part of the aircraft passenger seat unit. Dowty teaches away from including the forward cabin monument as part of the accommodation unit. Paragraph [0119] of Dowty states that the aft edge of a forward cabin monument (2104) can act as a forward boundary of the passenger suite 2100. Therefore, as can be seen in figs. 21A-21C, the forward cabin monument is not part of the passenger suite in the

disclosure of Dowty. Paragraphs [0123], [0127] and [0137] also state that the boundary of the passenger suite includes the aft ends of a forward cabin monument (2304, 2504 and 2704 respectively). Again, the skilled person would understand from Dowty that the forward cabin monument is not part of the passenger suite, so would not consider making changes to the forward cabin monument when designing a new passenger suite, and certainly not when considering changes relating to providing private storage to a passenger within the suite.
Kroll and Cailleteau fail to cure the aforementioned deficiencies of Dowty.

Therefore, the skilled person would simply not be motivated to adapt the passenger suite of Dowty to arrive at an aircraft passenger suite where the same door is movable in relation to the storage unit between a first position in which the door at least partially blocks off the primary opening, and a second position in which the door at least partially closes access to holders of the storage unit, wherein the front side of the storage unit provides access from the aircraft passenger seat unit to the holders of the storage unit.

For at least these reasons, claim 24 is allowable. Claims 25-31 and 33-37 are allowable because they depend from claim 24 and may be allowable for additional reasons. Withdrawal of the rejection is respectfully requested.
B. Claim 38

Applicant respectfully submits that the art of record fails to teach or suggest at least "a privacy shell at least partially surrounding the seat, the privacy shell being made up of a plurality of walls, including two parallel walls extending in the same plane, and having a primary opening between the two parallel walls to allow entry to and exit from the seat unit," "a door, movable between a first position in which the door at least partially blocks off the primary opening, and a second position, in which the door provides at least partial access to the primary opening," "the door is arranged to move between the first and second positions in a direction offset by an angle from the two parallel walls of the privacy shell," and "the door is angled relative to the two parallel walls of the privacy shell in the second position" as recited in claim 38.

In one instance, the Office Action rejects claim 38 in view of Cailleteau. Office Action page 3. In particular, and with reference to the below figure, the Office Action alleges that Cailleteau provides a seat 16, a privacy shell 18 with an opening having two edges, and a door 40. Id.

However, as illustrated in the above figure, Cailleteau discloses a seat unit in which a door is angled relative to the privacy shell in the first position (in which the door is closed, see vertical partition 40 of Fig. 9), but not in the second position. Moreover Cailleteau (in paragraph 7) teaches away from any alteration of a seat unit that reduces the space available within the seat unit. The skilled person would not consider modifying the door (vertical partition 40) of Cailleteau such that it is angled relative to the privacy shell in the second position because the door is stowed in a recess 42 of the privacy shell of the next-front seat unit. Modifying the angle of the door in the second position would therefore require reducing the space available within either the seat unit or the next-front seat unit. Alternatively, the skilled person would not consider adapting the door of Cailleteau to extend into the aisle of the seat unit as this would
reduce accessibility and passenger safety. For at least these reasons, Cailleteau fails to teach all aspects of claim 38, and claim 38 is allowable over Cailleteau.
In another instance, claim 38 is rejected based on the combination of Dowty, alone or in combination with Cailleteau. Office Action page 18.

However, there is no disclosure in Dowty of a seat unit with an opening between two parallel walls of a shell that extend in the same place and a door that is angled relative to the parallel walls of the privacy shell when the door is in the second position (in which the door provided at least partial access to the opening) as now recited in claim 38.

For example, in the embodiment of Fig 26E, the primary opening to the seat unit is not between two parallel walls extending in the same plane. Moreover, the skilled person would not consider altering the seat unit of Fig 26E to somehow include two such parallel walls, as this would require either extending the seat unit into the aisle of the aircraft (which would reduce the accessibility of the seat unit and decrease passenger safety) or altering the shape of the forward cabin monument (which the skilled person would not consider doing, as discussed above). There is further no teaching in Dowty that would lead the skilled person to adapt the door of Fig 26E to be angled relative to the walls of the shell in the second position.
As previously discussed, Cailleteau fails to teach similar features, and thus alone or in combination with Dowty, the prior art fails to teach the limitations of claim 38.

As neither Dowty nor Cailleteau would lead the skilled person to a seat unit in with the features of claim 38, it is submitted that claim 38 is not obvious in light of these documents, taken either individually or in combination.

For at least these reasons, claim 38 is allowable. Claims 39 and 40 are allowable because they depend from claim 38 and may be allowable for additional reasons. Withdrawal of the rejection is respectfully requested.

In view of the foregoing, Applicant believes all claims now pending in this application are in condition for allowance. The issuance of a formal Notice of Allowance at an early date is respectfully requested.
